root_cause.text: In `sev_ioctl_do_pek_csr()`, the code unconditionally copies the firmware-returned buffer length and data to userspace without first checking whether the PSP command actually succeeded, so a failed command (e.g., due to insufficient buffer) can cause the copy to read beyond the allocated kernel buffer, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds read and potential data leak.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE description states "If the failure was due to an invalid length, i.e. the userspace buffer+length was too small, copying the number of bytes _firmware_ requires will overflow the kernel-allocated buffer and leak data to userspace." The patch adds the check `if (ret || WARN_ON_ONCE(argp->error)) goto e_free_blob;` before copying the blob, confirming the missing error check is the root cause.

Copies the input structure (including the possibly invalid length) to userspace without verifying command success, leaking or exposing data beyond the kernel buffer.
Controls whether blob data is copied; while not directly responsible, it guards the subsequent copy that depends on the unchecked length.
Copies blob data to userspace using input.length derived from a command that may have failed, causing a slab-out-of-bounds read if the length is invalid.

vuln_statements.explanation: Unconditionally assigns the firmware-returned length into input without verifying whether the PSP command succeeded. If the command failed, data.len may be invalid or uninitialized, leading to an out-of-bounds read when this length is used later.

Copies the input structure (which contains the possibly invalid length) to userspace without checking that the command succeeded. This can leak kernel memory or cause out-of-bounds access if the length is corrupt.
Copies blob data to userspace using input.length derived from a potentially failed command. If the length is invalid, this results in a slab-out-of-bounds read from the kernel buffer.

Executes the PSP command; the return value indicates success or failure. Subsequent code ignores 'ret' and unconditionally uses the output data, enabling the out-of-bounds read when the command fails.
This conditional guards the second copy_to_user that uses input.length. While not directly vulnerable, it controls the code path that performs the slab-out-of-bounds read without a success check.
